README:
English** · 简体中文 · 繁體中文 · 日本語 · 한국어 · Türkçe · Русский · Tiếng Việt · ไทย · Deutsch · Español · Français · Українська · Polski · Português (Brasil) · العربية · فارسی · Bahasa Indonesia · Italiano

REA: Reverse Engineer Anything

One MCP for reverse engineering across binaries, applications, and runtime behavior.

See a feature you like. Understand how it works, down to the binary level.**

[](https://skills.sh/morluto/rea/reverse-engineer-anything)

Website · Guides · Showcases**

Quick start · How REA works · What you can analyze · Showcases · FAQ · Documentation

npx rea-agents setup

Join the Reverse Engineering Community
Discord · Q&A · Show and Tell

See a feature in an app that you want in your own product? Ask your agent to investigate it with REA. It can inspect the app without its source code, explain how the feature works, show the evidence, and build a version for your project.

REA connects your agent to tools for inspecting native binaries, JavaScript and Electron apps, .NET assemblies, and websites. You can also use the same tools from your terminal. Analysis runs locally, and results include the evidence and limitations behind each conclusion.

Setup registers REA with your agent and installs matching workflow instructions. Native analysis can use an existing Hopper, Ghidra, or IDA installation; setup can optionally install Hopper with approval. Static JavaScript analysis needs no native analysis engine.

Visit the REA website** for setup instructions, illustrated guides, and real case studies.

Update REA

To refresh your agent registrations and skill, run the setup command printed

If you use npx, update your agent setup with:

Review the setup changes and restart your agent. For one-off CLI commands,
use npx rea-agents@latest followed by the command. With Bun, use

How REA works

Your agent calls REA through MCP to inspect the target and trace relevant code.
REA returns findings with their evidence. The agent uses them to ask follow-up
questions, explain the behavior, or write and test an implementation.
CLI commands use the same workflows.

Open the full-size figure.

What you can analyze

REA requires Node.js 22.x (>=22.19), 24.x (>=24.11), or 26+, plus npm.
Additional tools and host support depend on the target:

| Target | What REA returns | Requirements and guide |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Native binaries | Pseudocode, assembly, strings, symbols, calls and references | Hopper, Ghidra or IDA; native analysis |
| Offline ELF layout | Sections, segments, original symbols/relocations and static mitigation candidates | Caller-supplied pwntools on Linux x64; binary diagnostics |
| Go binaries | Embedded compiler version, modules, replacements and build settings | Built-in static ELF/PE/thin Mach-O inspection; no Go installation required |
| WASM artifact | Validation, sections, exact import/export WAT forms and decoded WAT | Caller-supplied WABT 1.0.42; inspect_wasm_artifact |
| EVM bytecode | Dispatch selectors, byte offsets, inferred arguments and mutability | Local raw/hex carrier on Linux x64; offline EVM guide |
| SQLite databases | Tables, columns, indexes, views, triggers and selected ordinary-table rows | Local database/WAL snapshot; Node.js 24.x >=24.15 or 26+ with native SQLite limits |
| Recorded Linux crashes | Raw notes, every recorded thread's registers/signals and optional mapping candidates | Caller-supplied pwntools on Linux x64; optional GDB/pwndbg; recorded crashes |
| JavaScript / Electron | Modules, imports, source maps, routes, IPC and native add-on relationships | Node.js and npm; application analysis |
| Websites | Page structure, scripts, network observations and requested screenshots | A Chrome-family browser; browser analysis |
| Saved network captures | Requests, responses, exposed payloads and source locations | HAR; mitmdump on Linux for native mitmproxy captures; capture guide |
| .NET assemblies | Metadata, CIL instructions, declared native dependencies and build comparisons | None (static only); managed-code guide |
| Android APKs | Manifest declarations, classes, decompiled methods and references | Headless JADX and a full JDK on Linux/macOS/Windows x64; Android guide |
| Android devices | Devices, packages, processes, logs, dumps, screen captures, and APK/file transfers | Caller-supplied adb (emulator or hardware); ADB guide |
| JEB projects | Engine-backed project units, artifact digests and type/method pseudo-code | A caller-started JEB client serving MCP, selected with REA_JEB_MCP_URL; JEB guide |
| Android resources | Decoded manifest, string tables, locales and version facts | Caller-supplied Apktool launcher; resource guide |
| Flutter apps | Dart snapshot hash, per-ABI library digests and engine build provenance | None (static APK parsing); Flutter guide |
| Firmware | Regions, extraction results and native-analysis handoffs | Binwalk / Unblob on Linux; firmware guide |
| Recorded packets | Selected fields, repeated values, filters and decode-as rules | Linux: TShark 4.x + prlimit; capture guide |
| Recorded logic signals | Decoder annotations, sample ranges and diagnostics | Linux: sigrok-cli 0.7.2 + prlimit; signal recordings |
| Packages and resources | File inventories, digests, plists, Apple bundle anatomy and extracted resources | Artifact and JavaScript guide, Apple applications |
| Process behavior | Terminal output, interactions, exit and filesystem observations, and run comparisons | Linux/macOS with a native PTY; process capture |

Static JavaScript and .NET inspection read the supplied files without running
the application. Runtime capture runs or interacts with the selected target
using your user permissions; each runtime guide describes its effects.

Native formats and host support vary by provider. See
Hopper and Ghidra setup, the
IDA guide (including an optional native MCP bridge), and
experimental Windows Ghidra support.
Ghidra also supports 16-bit DOS analysis.
For large binaries, raise the provider's startup deadline with
REA_GHIDRA_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS or REA_HOPPER_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS.
For provider selection, see the CLI guide.
Check release availability
for features added since the latest npm release.

title: Accessing OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock with global cross-Region inference in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan
summary: Learn how to run OpenAI GPT-6 Sol, Luna, and Astra on Amazon Bedrock through global cross-Region inference from Singapore, Jakarta, Thailand, Malaysia, and Taipei. This post covers the Converse and OpenAI-compatible APIs, IAM and SCP permissions, quota sizing, and monitoring inference from your source Region.
content:
Single-Region inference can throttle when demand exceeds local capacity. Teams in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Taiwan need access to the newest OpenAI models beyond that capacity. Amazon Bedrock offers OpenAI GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna through global cross-Region inference from all five AWS Regions, and GPT-6 Astra from Asia Pacific (Singapore). This post shows you how to configure the call, set permissions, and monitor inference from your source Region.
GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6 Astra are all available through global cross-Region inference from the preceding Regions, on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. See Cross-Region inference in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. For the full list of source and destination Regions in each profile, see Supported Regions and models for inference profiles .
In this post, we introduce the global cross-Region inference profiles and invoke them from Asia Pacific (Singapore) using the Converse API, the OpenAI-compatible APIs, and coding clients. We then cover the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and service control policy (SCP) configuration, quota management, and monitoring.
Global cross-Region inference profiles for OpenAI GPT-6
The GPT-6 family offers three models, each available through global cross-Region inference.

GPT-6 Sol brings strong reasoning and coding capabilities to complex tasks performed throughout the week.
GPT-6 Luna makes focused, repeatable tasks practical at high volume.
GPT-6 Astra handles complex reasoning, coding, and long-document work.

All three accept text and image input, client-side tool use, and prompt caching. They differ on reasoning effort. GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna accept none, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. GPT-6 Astra accepts the same levels except none. For GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, see Bring more intelligence to everyday work with GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna on Amazon Bedrock . For GPT-6 Astra, see Take on your most ambitious work with GPT-6 Astra on Amazon Bedrock .
Global cross-Region inference routes requests across supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed, giving you broad access to Amazon Bedrock capacity. You invoke it by passing a global cross-Region inference profile ID in place of a model ID. Your source Region is where you make the API call. Amazon Bedrock selects the destination Region for processing. Billing, quota tracking, AWS CloudTrail, and Amazon CloudWatch all stay in your source Region.
The following table lists the global cross-Region inference profile IDs and the source Regions covered in this post.

Global cross-Region inference profiles
Source Regions
Destination Regions

global.openai.gpt-6-sol
global.openai.gpt-6-luna

Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1
Asia Pacific (Jakarta) ap-southeast-3
Asia Pacific (Malaysia) ap-southeast-5
Asia Pacific (Thailand) ap-southeast-7
Asia Pacific (Taipei) ap-east-2

Supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed

global.openai.gpt-6-astra
Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1
Supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed

Inference profile availability and Region support change as AWS adds Regions and profiles, so confirm both on the model card before you build: GPT-6 Sol , GPT-6 Luna , and GPT-6 Astra . For per-token rates, see Amazon Bedrock pricing .
Getting started with OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock
Start with the prerequisites, then invoke any of the three profiles through the Converse API, the OpenAI-compatible APIs, or your existing coding client.
Prerequisites

An IAM identity with permission to invoke the profile. The IAM policy in the Security and permissions section grants only what these examples need.
Your source Region activated. Only the Region you call from needs activating. You do not activate destination Regions, which run on Amazon Bedrock managed capacity. Singapore ( ap-southeast-1 ) is a Region that is enabled by default. Jakarta ( ap-southeast-3 ), Malaysia ( ap-southeast-5 ), Thailand ( ap-southeast-7 ), and Taipei ( ap-east-2 ) are opt-in Regions you must activate first. For more information, see Enable or disable AWS Regions in your account .
A current AWS SDK or CLI. The OpenAI-compatible examples also require the OpenAI SDK and the Amazon Bedrock token generator. Install them with pip install boto3 openai aws-bedrock-token-generator .

The Amazon Bedrock console lists all three global cross-Region inference profiles under system-defined inference profiles. See Figure 1.

Figure 1: The three global OpenAI GPT-6 inference profiles among the system-defined profiles in the Amazon Bedrock console

Invoke GPT-6 models through Amazon Bedrock Runtime
Each model supports three access paths on this endpoint: the Amazon Bedrock Converse API, the OpenAI Responses API, and the OpenAI Chat Completions API. The OpenAI-compatible APIs are called on the /openai/v1 paths rather than through the AWS SDKs, and the endpoint accepts either Signature Version 4 (SigV4) or an Amazon Bedrock API key. Pass the global cross-Region inference profile ID as the model in every case.
Converse API. This example calls GPT-6 Sol from Asia Pacific (Singapore) and logs the response. Set BEDROCK_PROFILE_ID to global.openai.gpt-6-luna or global.openai.gpt-6-astra to switch models, or call converse_stream for streaming.

import logging
import os
import boto3

# AWS_REGION overrides this default, so set it to your source Region or unset it.
REGION = os.environ.get("AWS_REGION", "ap-southeast-1")
PROFILE_ID = os.environ.get("BEDROCK_PROFILE_ID", "global.openai.gpt-6-sol")
PROMPT = (
"In three bullet points, explain when a workload should use "
"cross-Region inference instead of calling a model in a single Region."
)

logging.basicConfig(format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("bedrock-cris")
log.setLevel(logging.INFO)

client = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name=REGION)

# AccessDeniedException points at the IAM policy. ValidationException usually
# means the model ID is not a global cross-Region inference profile.
response = client.converse(
modelId=PROFILE_ID,
messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": PROMPT}]}],
inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 1024},
# GPT-6 Sol and Luna accept none through max. GPT-6 Astra rejects none.
additionalModelRequestFields={"reasoning": {"effort": "low"}},
)

# Any effort above none can prepend a reasoningContent block, so pick the text
# block by key rather than by position.
text = "".join(b["text"] for b in response["output"]["message"]["content"] if "text" in b)

log.info("Called %s from %s", PROFILE_ID, REGION)
log.info("Stop reason: %s", response["stopReason"])
log.info("Response:\n%s", text)

OpenAI Chat Completions API. Point the OpenAI SDK at the Regional endpoint and pass the same profile ID.

import logging
import os
from aws_bedrock_token_generator import provide_token
from openai import OpenAI

REGION = os.environ.get("AWS_REGION", "ap-southeast-1")
PROFILE_ID = os.environ.get("BEDROCK_PROFILE_ID", "global.openai.gpt-6-sol")
PROMPT = "List three uses for a message queue."

logging.basicConfig(format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("bedrock-cris")
log.setLevel(logging.INFO)

# provide_token mints a short-term key from your AWS credentials, valid up to 12 hours.
client = OpenAI(
base_url=f"https://bedrock-runtime.{REGION}.amazonaws.com/openai/v1",
api_key=provide_token(region=REGION),
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
model=PROFILE_ID,
messages=[{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT}],
max_completion_tokens=256,
)

log.info("Called %s from %s", PROFILE_ID, REGION)
log.info("Response:\n%s", response.choices[0].message.content)

When migrating an existing OpenAI client:

Set the model parameter on every request, including those referencing a previous response.
Use supported tool types: function , mcp , custom , namespace , and tool_search .
Configure the inference profile ID directly in your client rather than querying the models endpoint.

Set up the ChatGPT desktop app and Codex CLI
The ChatGPT desktop app and the Codex CLI share ~/.codex/config.toml , so one change covers both. Of the two built-in Amazon Bedrock providers, only amazon-bedrock-runtime accepts an inference profile.

model = "global.openai.gpt-6-astra"
model_provider = "amazon-bedrock-runtime"
[model_providers.amazon-bedrock-runtime.aws]
region = "ap-southeast-1"

SigV4 signing means there is no key to rotate. Add profile = "<your-profile>" for a non-default profile, and set region explicitly, because the client otherwise falls back to AWS_REGION . Substitute another profile ID for model to change models.
Codex reports a 272,000-token window for these profiles, which is its own bundled figure rather than a service limit. Raise it with model_context_window . This configuration needs Codex CLI 0.148 or later.
Figure 2 shows the result in the app.

Figure 2: The ChatGPT desktop app running GPT-6 Astra on Amazon Bedrock

Security and permissions
Amazon Bedrock offers a range of controls over inference. Two of them matter here. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies control which roles can invoke which profiles, and service control policies (SCPs) apply organization-wide controls, including Region scope. This section covers both, and where request data lands.
IAM permissions for global cross-Region inference
To call any of these models through a global cross-Region inference profile, your IAM policy needs four statements:

Access to the inference profile and the project/default resource in your source Region.
Access to the foundation model in your source Region, scoped to the inference profile.
The Region-agnostic Amazon Resource Name (ARN) for the foundation model, arn:aws:bedrock:::foundation-model/openai.gpt-6-sol , with aws:RequestedRegion set to unspecified to permit cross-Region routing.
bedrock:CallWithBearerToken for API-key authentication.

This IAM policy grants permission to invoke GPT-6 Sol through global cross-Region inference from ap-southeast-1 . Replace with your AWS account ID and ap-southeast-1 with your source Region.

{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "GrantGlobalCrisProfileAndProjectAccess",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": ["bedrock:InvokeModel"],
"Resource": [
"arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-1:<ACCOUNT>:inference-profile/global.openai.gpt-6-sol",
"arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-1:<ACCOUNT>:project/default"
],
"Condition": {
"StringEquals": { "aws:RequestedRegion": "ap-southeast-1" }
}
},
{
"Sid": "GrantGlobalCrisInRegionModelAccess",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": ["bedrock:InvokeModel"],
"Resource": ["arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-1::foundation-model/openai.gpt-6-sol"],
"Condition": {
"StringEquals": {
"aws:RequestedRegion": "ap-southeast-1",
"bedrock:InferenceProfileArn": "arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-1:<ACCOUNT>:inference-profile/global.openai.gpt-6-sol"
}
}
},
{
"Sid": "GrantGlobalCrisGlobalModelAccess",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": ["bedrock:InvokeModel"],
"Resource": ["arn:aws:bedrock:::foundation-model/openai.gpt-6-sol"],
"Condition": {
"StringEquals": {
"aws:RequestedRegion": "unspecified",
"bedrock:InferenceProfileArn": "arn:aws:bedrock:ap-southeast-1:<ACCOUNT>:inference-profile/global.openai.gpt-6-sol"
}
}
},
{
"Sid": "AllowBearerTokenAuth",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": ["bedrock:CallWithBearerToken"],
"Resource": "*"
}
]
}

If you use streaming ( converse_stream or stream=True ), add bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream to the Action in the first three statements. Converse authorizes as bedrock:InvokeModel . If you only call Converse with SigV4 credentials, drop the fourth statement.
To switch models, replace openai.gpt-6-sol with openai.gpt-6-luna or openai.gpt-6-astra throughout. For the complete reference, see IAM policy requirements for global cross-Region inference .
Service control policy considerations for global cross-Region inference
A global cross-Region inference request carries no Region name. Amazon Bedrock sets aws:RequestedRegion to unspecified , so a Region allowlist in an SCP denies the call, and the error names only the policy type, not which policy. That is a common reason a first call fails in an enterprise account.
Rather than widening the allowlist, scope the exception. Amazon Bedrock populates the bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition key during authorization, so an SCP can allow these profiles while keeping Region controls for everything else. The following SCP does that.

{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "DenyOutsideApprovedRegionsExceptBedrockInvoke",
"Effect": "Deny",
"NotAction": [
"iam:*", "sts:*", "organizations:*", "account:*",
"route53:*", "cloudfront:*", "waf:*", "wafv2:*", "shield:*",
"support:*", "trustedadvisor:*", "health:*",
"budgets:*", "ce:*", "cur:*", "tax:*", "billing:*",
"bedrock:Invoke*"
],
"Resource": "*",
"Condition": {
"StringNotEquals": { "aws:RequestedRegion": ["ap-southeast-1"] }
}
},
{
"Sid": "DenyBedrockInferenceOutsideApprovedRegionsUnlessCris",
"Effect": "Deny",
"Action": ["bedrock:Invoke*"],
"Resource": "*",
"Condition": {
"StringNotEquals": { "aws:RequestedRegion": ["ap-southeast-1"] },
"ArnNotLike": {
"bedrock:InferenceProfileArn": [
"arn:aws:bedrock:*:*:inference-profile/global.*"
]
}
}
}
]
}

The first statement enforces your Region allowlist for every service except Amazon Bedrock inference. The second denies that inference outside those Regions unless it routes through a global cross-Region inference profile. For geographic profiles, add their prefix (for example inference-profile/us.* ) to the ArnNotLike list, because geographic requests carry a real Region name. Keep your source Region in the allowlist, and add the global services your organization uses to NotAction .
A blunter alternative is to add unspecified to your existing allowlist, which works but opens the same exception to every other service. For a ready-to-use policy file, see the aws-samples service-control-policy-examples repository .
Data retention and abuse detection
For automated offline abuse detection, classifier-flagged traffic is retained by AWS for up to 30 days and processed programmatically. Under cross-Region inference that retention happens in the destination Region, which for a global profile is any supported commercial AWS Region where the model is deployed. Eligible customers might request full zero data retention through their AWS account team. For more information, see Amazon Bedrock abuse detection and Data retention .
If your organization has data residency requirements, take this to your risk and compliance team early. See the AWS Financial Services Compliance Center country pages for these five countries. We recommend you obtain your own advice on compliance with the requirements relevant to your business.
Quota management
GPT-6 quotas on bedrock-runtime are measured in tokens per minute (TPM), tracked against the source Region you call from. Input and cache-write tokens count 1:1, and each output token consumes 10 tokens of quota. For example, a request with 2,000 input tokens and 1,000 output tokens depletes 12,000 tokens from your quota.
Amazon Bedrock reserves the full max_tokens up front, so set it close to the completions you expect. One quota covers InvokeModel , Converse, Responses, and Chat Completions. Review and raise it on the Service Quotas console from your source Region. Before production, request increases early and alarm on EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage in the AWS/Bedrock namespace at 70–80 percent of your allocation. See How tokens are counted in Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock endpoints and quotas for current values.
Monitoring and logging
Your operational surface stays in your source Region. Amazon CloudWatch metrics, AWS CloudTrail events, model invocation logs, quota accounting, and billing all remain in the Region you called from. You pay that Region’s rates, not the processing Region’s.
CloudTrail records where each request was processed. AWS documents a global cross-Region inference profile’s destinations as its commercial Regions rather than enumerating them. GetInferenceProfile returns the Region-agnostic and source-Region model ARNs rather than a destination list. Your per-request record is additionalEventData.inferenceRegion in CloudTrail in your source Region. Inference on this endpoint is a management event, logged by default at no extra cost. CloudTrail Event History retains 90 days, so longer horizons need a trail or model invocation logging. Retrieve the CloudTrail events with this command.

aws cloudtrail lookup-events \
--region ap-southeast-1 \
--lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventSource,AttributeValue=bedrock.amazonaws.com \
--start-time <START> \
--end-time <END> \
--max-results 1 \
--query 'Events[0].CloudTrailEvent' --output text | python3 -m json.tool

Set the window around a call you just made, because CloudTrail delivery lags by a few minutes. If the most recent event was a failed call, it carries an errorCode and no inferenceRegion . Raise --max-results and pick an event without errorCode .

{
"eventName": "Converse",
"eventSource": "bedrock.amazonaws.com",
"awsRegion": "ap-southeast-1",
"managementEvent": true,
"requestParameters": {
"modelId": "global.openai.gpt-6-sol",
"inferenceConfig": { "maxTokens": 1024 }
},
"additionalEventData": {
"inferenceRegion": "us-east-1"
}
}

Metrics and coding-agent usage stay in CloudWatch. Where developers reach GPT-6 through a coding agent, CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights adds ready-made dashboards under GenAI Observability that break token use down by user, team, and cost center. The agents emit OpenTelemetry metrics natively. For Codex, see Set up OpenTelemetry for OpenAI Codex .
Clean up
This post adds an IAM policy and optionally an SCP statement and a logging destination. Detach or delete the IAM policy you attached, and revert the SCP entry if you added one. Delete the model invocation logging destination in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch Logs if you created one, to avoid storage charges. The global cross-Region inference profiles are system-defined, so there is nothing to delete.
Conclusion
This post showed how to invoke GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna from five Asia Pacific source Regions, and GPT-6 Astra from Asia Pacific (Singapore), through global cross-Region inference on bedrock-runtime . Pass a global cross-Region inference profile ID as the model parameter, and configure the IAM policy and SCP exception from this post. The same endpoint serves the OpenAI-compatible APIs, so an existing OpenAI integration moves across by changing a base URL and a key.
To get started, attach the IAM policy from this post, and send a first request through global.openai.gpt-6-sol . Size your tokens-per-minute quota at the 10x burndown rate, and confirm in CloudTrail that additionalEventData.inferenceRegion appears on your calls.
For more information, see the Amazon Bedrock User Guide , Route model inference requests across AWS Regions with cross-Region inference , and Amazon Bedrock pricing .
 

About the authors

Traci Lim
Traci is a Senior AI/ML Specialist Technical Account Manager at AWS based in Singapore. A machine learning engineer by trade, he works with startups and enterprises to operationalize and scale AI/ML applications in production, with a focus on GenAIOps, Agentic Ops, operational excellence, and cost and performance optimization. Prior to AWS, Traci led engineering teams in the tech and financial industries, scaling distributed AI systems across AWS, Azure, GCP, and SAP. He is a builder at heart, always looking for ways to create meaningful impact through technology.

He likes to stay hands-on, getting into the details and building out solutions that solve real operational problems.

Melanie, PhD, is a Senior Generative AI Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS based in Sydney, Australia, where her focus is on working with customers to build solutions using state-of-the-art AI/ML tools. She has been actively involved in multiple generative AI initiatives across APJ, harnessing the power of LLMs. Prior to joining AWS, Dr. Li held data science roles in the financial and retail industries.

title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
summary:
StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutoring tools before they are tested with learners. It models how individuals may engage with tutors, giving feedback to improve tutor performance across subjects like chess, writing, and mathematics.
The post Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring appeared first on Microsoft Research .
content:
At a glance

StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutors before they are tested with real learners; it is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and is not intended to replace teachers

AI tutoring tools need feedback from students to improve, but collecting that feedback through human studies is slow, costly, and difficult to scale 

StudentSim trains personalized AI student simulators from publicly available, de-identified learner records, with one simulator adapted to each student 

The work evaluates simulators along two education-grounded dimensions: whether they respond like a specific student, and whether they update after tutor guidance 

Across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, StudentSim outperforms leading baselines and provides a useful feedback signal for training an AI tutor 

In research settings, teams are exploring how AI-powered tutoring systems can help explain a math problem, suggest an edit to a writing assignment, or guide a learner through a chess position. Yet the quality of teaching cannot be measured only from the tutor’s answer. A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student. Did the student correct the original mistake? Did the hint help them reason toward the answer, or did it give away too much? Would a different student need a different kind of support? In today’s AI tutor research, answering these questions often requires real learner studies. Those studies are valuable, but they are slow and costly to run, which makes it hard to use student feedback during fast model iteration.

StudentSim is an AI system that creates personalized simulators of individual students, modeling how they answer questions and how their answers change after receiving a tutor’s guidance. The goal is to make student feedback more available during AI tutor development. This research also introduces StudentSimEval, a benchmark and evaluation protocol spanning chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics. 

Importantly, the goal is not to replace teachers or classroom learning. Instead, StudentSim helps researchers evaluate and improve AI tutoring systems during the research and development process before testing them with real learners. The research uses only publicly available learner datasets released for research use with de-identified records; no personally identifying information is used at any stage. 

Figure 1: AI tutors need feedback from students to improve. Student simulators can approximate part of that feedback during research-stage training and evaluation. They provide an early-stage research signal, not a replacement for testing with real learners.

Measuring what a student simulator needs to do

A simple way to build a student simulator is to ask a large language model to role-play a learner. For example, a prompt might say, “You are an elementary-school student who struggles with math.” The model can change its tone and express uncertainty. The harder part is preserving the learner’s actual ability boundary. A model may speak in a young student’s voice while still relying on knowledge and reasoning far beyond that student’s level. For training an AI tutor, this can produce misleading feedback: the tutor may appear effective because the simulated student is too capable.

Traditional student modeling approaches face a different limitation. Knowledge tracing and behavior prediction models are grounded in real learning records and can estimate a student’s current knowledge, skills, and learning habits. Many of these models, however, were not designed to take natural-language tutor guidance as input. They can help describe what a student has done, but they do not always tell us how a student would respond to a particular explanation, hint, or Socratic question.

StudentSim defines the target through two dimensions inspired by education research. Educators often distinguish what a learner can do independently from what they can do with support. Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development captures this gap between current independent performance and performance with guidance. StudentSim turns this idea into two evaluation goals. Behavioral fidelity measures whether a simulator matches a specific student’s recorded responses on held-out problems. Guidance responsiveness measures whether the simulator updates its response after reading tutor guidance.

Figure 2: StudentSimEval evaluates whether a simulator matches a student’s independent behavior and whether it responds to guidance.  

These two goals are complementary. A simulator that only matches past student behavior may be useful for prediction, but it does not show whether a teaching intervention helped. A simulator that always follows the tutor may respond fluently, but it may fail to represent a particular student’s strengths, weaknesses, and likely mistakes. AI tutor training needs both signals: the learner’s starting point and how guidance affects the learner’s performance. 

Training personalized simulators from sparse student records

StudentSimEval is built entirely from publicly available learner datasets that are released for research use with de-identified records. The records carry no personally identifying information, and each personalized simulator is trained only on the de-identified records of the student it represents.

Real student data is often sparse at the individual level. A learner may contribute only a small number of essays, answers, or interactions. Training a separate simulator from scratch for each student would risk overfitting and would require each model to relearn common patterns in the domain.  

StudentSim uses a two-stage training pipeline. In the first stage, the model trains on records pooled across many students in the same domain. This stage learns common response formats, common errors, and common ways students revise after guidance. In the second stage, the model is specialized on one student’s own records, producing a personalized simulator for that student. 

Figure 3: StudentSim first learns shared student behavior from pooled records, then adapts to each student’s own data.  

The evaluation covers three domains with different response types. In chess, the simulator predicts a player’s next move and how that player may revise after coaching. In second-language English writing, it generates essays with error patterns matching a learner and predicts corrections after teacher feedback. In mathematics, it predicts a student’s multiple-choice answer and whether the student updates after an explanation. Across these domains, StudentSimEval uses the same principle: compare all methods on the same per-student training records and the same held-out evaluation records. 

StudentSim outperforms leading baselines across the three domains. In chess, for example, StudentSim reaches behavioral fidelity of 0.5150 and guidance responsiveness of 0.9067. GPT-5.4 reaches 0.2316 and 0.7186, respectively. Maia2, a chess-specific human move prediction model, reaches 0.4535 and 0.2721. The comparison illustrates the difference between the baseline families: GPT-5.4 can respond to guidance but does not reliably match a specific student’s behavior, while Maia2 predicts human chess moves more closely but lacks a natural-language guidance pathway.

Figure 4: In chess, StudentSim improves both behavioral fidelity and guidance responsiveness compared with leading baselines.

Using simulated feedback to improve AI tutors

The research also tests whether a trained student simulator can provide feedback for tutor optimization. In a chess tutor reinforcement learning study, the tutor receives a position and a real student’s previous wrong move, then generates guidance. The student simulator’s own parameters are held fixed during this process, and it reads the guidance and produces a revised move. The reward is based on the improvement in move quality from the student’s previous move to the simulator’s revised move, using Stockfish as an independent chess engine signal.  

Figure 5: StudentSim can provide feedback during AI tutor reinforcement learning by estimating how a student response changes after guidance.

The study compares three conditions: a supervised fine-tuned tutor with no reinforcement learning, a tutor trained with GPT-5.4 as the simulated student reward source, and a tutor trained with StudentSim as the reward source. All conditions use the same tutor policy, supervised starting point, and reinforcement learning setup. Human chess experts then evaluate the tutor responses blind to condition. 

The StudentSim reward produces the highest-rated tutor on all reported dimensions. The tutor trained with StudentSim reaches 90.5% accuracy, compared with 75.7% for the no-RL baseline and 71.6% for the GPT-5.4 reward condition. It also receives higher ratings for guidance quality and personalization. The result is a proof of concept that student simulators trained on real learner data can provide useful feedback for improving AI tutors. 

Looking ahead

StudentSim does not remove the need for real learners in education research. Human studies remain essential for measuring learning outcomes, safety, usability, and classroom fit. The role of student simulators is earlier in the development process: they can help researchers test tutor strategies, compare models, and refine training signals before moving to more expensive studies with real students. 

The broader direction is to build AI tutor systems that learn from student reactions, not only from expert-written explanations or static correctness labels. StudentSim shows one path: use real learning records to train personalized simulators, evaluate those simulators on both independent behavior and response to guidance, and use them as scalable feedback sources for tutor training. Future work can extend this approach to longer learning trajectories, additional subjects, richer student profiles, and studies that connect simulated feedback with real learning outcomes. 

The paper and the StudentSim training and evaluation code, including the StudentSimEval protocol, are publicly available.

title: Deploy decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI
summary: Learn how to deploy decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI. This technical how-to serves OpenAI-compatible chat completions with the AWS Deep Learning Container for llama.cpp, then extends the runtime with SemIf to return probabilities over declared options on CPU or GPU.
content:
Applications that route requests, select agent actions, or assign policy outcomes often need scores over a fixed set of choices instead of free-form text. Deploying these decision models with llama.cpp on Amazon SageMaker AI gives you a managed path for serving quantized models on CPU or GPU infrastructure.
This post continues a series on specialized AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) for generative AI inference. Previous posts cover WhisperX , vLLM-Omni – Part 1 , and vLLM-Omni – Part 2 .
In this post, you first use the AWS DLC for llama.cpp to serve OpenAI-compatible chat completions through SageMaker AI InvokeEndpoint . You then extend the same runtime with SemIf , formerly OpenJev, which returns probabilities over declared options without decoding an answer token. The accompanying code sample includes CPU and GPU deployment options.
Solution overview
Figure 1 shows two deployment paths from the same packaged model. The text-generation path uses the AWS DLC for llama.cpp and returns generated responses through the OpenAI-compatible API. The structured-decision path builds a child image that replaces the default server with a SemIf adapter and returns probabilities for declared options.

Figure 1: Run the AWS DLC for llama.cpp or the SemIf child image on CPU or GPU, depending on the API and latency requirements of your workload

For the standard path, package the model as model.tar.gz in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and reference the published DLC image directly. The container finds the first .gguf file under /opt/ml/model , maps POST /invocations to llama-server at /v1/chat/completions , and passes SM_LLAMA_CPP_* environment variables to llama.cpp arguments.
The llama-server HTTP API doesn’t expose the final-position logits and state operations that SemIf uses. The structured-decision path therefore uses AWS CodeBuild to build a child image and store it in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) . The child image keeps the DLC’s compiled CPU or CUDA libraries while replacing its entry point with a SageMaker-compatible adapter.
Understand the input and output schemas
The AWS DLC for llama.cpp accepts the OpenAI Chat Completions schema. Send a messages array with role and content , plus generation controls such as max_tokens and stream :

{
"messages": [
{
"role": "user",
"content": "A customer cannot receive a password reset email. Reply with the best support queue."
}
],
"max_tokens": 64,
"stream": false
}

The response uses the OpenAI-compatible choices array. Read generated text from choices[0].message.content .
SemIf uses a constrained decision schema instead of chat messages. The request contains a caller-defined ID, unstructured state, a question, and an ordered list of allowed options:

{
"decision": {
"id": "support-route",
"state": "The customer cannot receive a password reset email.",
"question": "Which queue should handle this request?",
"options": [
{"id": "account_access", "description": "Account access support."},
{"id": "billing", "description": "Billing support."}
]
}
}

The response returns option_ids , probabilities , and raw option_logits in the same order, along with prompt, timing, and pinned model metadata. With stable option IDs, your application can apply thresholds, fallbacks, and policy checks without parsing generated prose.
SemIf belongs to a broader class of decision models that score application-defined outcomes from unstructured state. Other implementations include Jev , TypeSafe’s decision model and /v1/systemone API; Kev , a model server designed for TypeSafe API compatibility; and Strands Decider 2B , a purpose-built model for agent workflows with calibrated outputs.
Choose the right decision workflows
Use this pattern when your application defines the allowed choices at request time and needs a model to interpret unstructured context. Examples include routing a case to a queue, extracting one value from a known set, assigning an incident priority, checking a policy outcome, or selecting an agent action. Keep authorization and deterministic business rules outside the model, and validate model probabilities before treating them as operational confidence.
Use the standard SageMaker AI text-generation path when you need OpenAI-compatible chat completions through InvokeEndpoint . The SageMaker AI image maps POST /invocations to the llama-server /v1/chat/completions endpoint. Build a child image only when your application needs behavior that this interface doesn’t provide, such as SemIf’s direct logits and state access.
Removing answer-token generation doesn’t remove model inference. The model still processes the complete state, question, and option descriptions before SemIf reads the final logits. Keep prompts focused, and evaluate the selected model with labeled decisions from your application before production use.
Tune for your latency and quality targets
The following benchmark applies to the SemIf extension, not the text-generation endpoint. Model size, quantization, prompt length, runtime, and CPU thread count affect each decision. To quantify these trade-offs, we sent the same 231 public JevBench tasks serially to one CPU endpoint and one GPU endpoint.

Configuration
AWS DLC for llama.cpp

Client p95

llama-cpp:server-sagemaker-cpu-v1

Compared with the CPU configuration, the GPU endpoint was 4.9 times faster at p50 and 32.2 times faster at p95. The sample uses the SageMaker AI instance pools feature to list compatible GPU instance types in priority order, so SageMaker can select an alternative when the first preference isn’t available. The pool ordered g6e , g6 , g5 , then g4dn . SageMaker selected ml.g6e.xlarge , and startup logs confirmed that llama.cpp offloaded all 34 model layers to an NVIDIA L40S. The CPU and GPU images used different llama.cpp builds and produced different predictions on six hard tasks. Treat the one-answer accuracy difference as runtime variation, not evidence that GPU offload improves model quality.
Smaller models reduced median latency, but the 2B and 0.8B candidates achieved 66.7 percent and 58.4 percent accuracy. The sample therefore keeps the 4B Q4_K_M model as its quality-first default. These measurements include network latency and aren’t service guarantees.
Benchmark the complete model and infrastructure configuration against your own decisions. Use CPU for background, offline, or low-throughput workloads that aren’t latency-sensitive and can tolerate seconds of response time. Use GPU for interactive decisions, long prompts, or workloads with tight tail-latency targets. Keep state and option descriptions concise, group decisions that share the same state into one request, and scale endpoint instances for concurrency. Shared-state scoring reuses the common prompt prefix, while the adapter returns retryable HTTP 503 responses instead of allowing an unbounded queue around its stateful llama.cpp context.
Prerequisites
You need:

An AWS account and an S3 bucket in your deployment AWS Region.
Python 3.10 or later, Git, and the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI).
A purpose-specific CodeBuild service role for the optional SemIf extension.
An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that SageMaker AI can assume.
Permissions for SageMaker AI, Amazon ECR, Amazon S3, CodeBuild, IAM pass-role actions, and Amazon CloudWatch Logs .
Quota for a compatible x86 CPU or NVIDIA GPU SageMaker real-time endpoint.

The text-generation example uses the CPU DLC and a fixed CPU instance. The SemIf extension keeps CPU as the default for workloads that aren’t latency-sensitive and offers an optional CUDA image with ordered instance pools. Review SageMaker AI pricing before creating an endpoint.
Deploy a decision model and extend it with SemIf
Use the following procedure to deploy the standard text-generation endpoint, then build the optional SemIf extension for structured decisions on CPU or GPU.

Clone the code sample and install its dependencies.

git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sagemaker-genai-hosting-examples.git
cd sagemaker-genai-hosting-examples/03-features/semif-decision-model
python3 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python3 -m pip install -r deploy/requirements.txt

Set the deployment values for your account.

export AWS_REGION="<your-region>"
export ARTIFACT_BUCKET=amzn-s3-demo-semif-artifacts
export CODEBUILD_ROLE_ARN=arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/semif-codebuild-role
export SAGEMAKER_ROLE_ARN=arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/semif-sagemaker-role
export STANDARD_ENDPOINT_NAME=llamacpp-gguf
export SEMIF_ENDPOINT_NAME=semif-decision-workflows

Package the pinned GGUF model and tokenizer with CodeBuild.

python deploy/prepare_model_build.py \
--region "$AWS_REGION" \
--bucket "$ARTIFACT_BUCKET" \
--codebuild-role-arn "$CODEBUILD_ROLE_ARN" \
--model-s3-uri "s3://$ARTIFACT_BUCKET/semif-llamacpp/model.tar.gz"

Wait for the returned build ID to reach SUCCEEDED . The build records the source revisions and checksums in model-manifest.json and stops if the GGUF checksum differs from the validated value.
Deploy the GGUF model with the AWS DLC for llama.cpp.
Resolve a digest-pinned server-sagemaker-cpu-v1 image from the AWS DLC for llama.cpp documentation , then create the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint:

export STANDARD_IMAGE_URI="<published-llama-cpp-cpu-image>@sha256:<digest>"

python deploy/deploy_standard_endpoint.py \
--region "$AWS_REGION" \
--image-uri "$STANDARD_IMAGE_URI" \
--model-data-url "s3://$ARTIFACT_BUCKET/semif-llamacpp/model.tar.gz" \
--role-arn "$SAGEMAKER_ROLE_ARN" \
--instance-type ml.c6i.2xlarge \
--name "$STANDARD_ENDPOINT_NAME"

Select a server-sagemaker-cpu-v1 or server-sagemaker-cuda-v1 image rather than the corresponding EC2 image. The SageMaker AI images implement the /ping and /invocations container contract and map invocation payloads to chat completions.
This walkthrough supplies the GGUF model through the SageMaker AI model artifact in Amazon S3. As an alternative, you can configure SM_LLAMA_CPP_HF_REPO and SM_LLAMA_CPP_HF_FILE to download a GGUF file from Hugging Face when the endpoint has network egress.
You don’t need a Dockerfile or an ECR repository for this path. Wait for the endpoint to enter InService , then send an OpenAI-compatible chat request:

python deploy/invoke_standard_endpoint.py \
--region "$AWS_REGION" \
--endpoint-name "$STANDARD_ENDPOINT_NAME"

Build the optional SemIf child image and resolve its immutable digest.
For CPU:

python deploy/prepare_build.py \
--region "$AWS_REGION" \
--bucket "$ARTIFACT_BUCKET" \
--codebuild-role-arn "$CODEBUILD_ROLE_ARN"

For GPU, build the CUDA child image instead:

python deploy/prepare_build.py \
--region "$AWS_REGION" \
--bucket "$ARTIFACT_BUCKET" \
--codebuild-role-arn "$CODEBUILD_ROLE_ARN" \
--dockerfile Dockerfile.gpu \
--image-tag "gpu-$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)"

After the build succeeds, construct the immutable image URI:

ECR_REPOSITORY_URI=$(aws ecr describe-repositories \
--region "$AWS_REGION" \
--repository-names semif-llamacpp-dlc \
--query 'repositories[0].repositoryUri' \
--output text)
IMAGE_DIGEST=$(aws ecr describe-images \
--region "$AWS_REGION" \
--repository-name semif-llamacpp-dlc \
--query 'sort_by(imageDetails,&imagePushedAt)[-1].imageDigest' \
--output text)
export IMAGE_URI="${ECR_REPOSITORY_URI}@${IMAGE_DIGEST}"

The deployment script rejects mutable image tags.
Deploy the SemIf endpoint.
The CPU configuration uses a fixed instance type:

python deploy/deploy_endpoint.py \
--region "$AWS_REGION" \
--image-uri "$IMAGE_URI" \
--model-data-url "s3://$ARTIFACT_BUCKET/semif-llamacpp/model.tar.gz" \
--role-arn "$SAGEMAKER_ROLE_ARN" \
--instance-type ml.c6i.8xlarge \
--threads 32 \
--name "$SEMIF_ENDPOINT_NAME"

Wait for the returned endpoint name to enter InService . This path sets n_gpu_layers=0 . The adapter serializes scoring around one stateful llama.cpp context, so scale out with endpoint instances after measuring your workload rather than assuming parallel scoring inside one container.
For the GPU image, provide ordered instance pools and request full model offload:

python deploy/deploy_endpoint.py \
--region "$AWS_REGION" \
--image-uri "$IMAGE_URI" \
--model-data-url "s3://$ARTIFACT_BUCKET/semif-llamacpp/model.tar.gz" \
--role-arn "$SAGEMAKER_ROLE_ARN" \
--instance-pool ml.g6e.xlarge \
--instance-pool ml.g6.2xlarge \
--instance-pool ml.g5.2xlarge \
--instance-pool ml.g4dn.2xlarge \
--gpu-layers=-1 \
--provision-timeout 1200 \
--name "$SEMIF_ENDPOINT_NAME"

Instance pools are ordered placement fallbacks, not inference load balancing. SageMaker selects one available type for the variant. Endpoint creation can take longer while SageMaker AI works through the pool. Check the startup logs for the selected GPU and a message confirming that all model layers were offloaded.
Invoke the SemIf endpoint with the example decision.
The request declares stable IDs for each allowed option:

{
"decision": {
"id": "support-route",
"state": "Customer asks to reset a forgotten password and says the reset email never arrived.",
"question": "Which queue should handle this request?",
"options": [
{"id": "account_access", "description": "Account access and authentication support."},
{"id": "billing", "description": "Billing and payment support."},
{"id": "sales", "description": "Sales and product evaluation."}
]
}
}

python deploy/invoke_endpoint.py \
--region "$AWS_REGION" \
--endpoint-name "$SEMIF_ENDPOINT_NAME"

The response preserves the option order and includes conditional probabilities, raw logits, token and prompt metadata, and the pinned model identity:

{
"result": {
"id": "support-route",
"option_ids": ["account_access", "billing", "sales"],
"probabilities": [0.99996, 0.00003, 0.00001],
"option_logits": [28.47, 17.92, 17.04],
"prompt_sha256": "016267542103ab91422c425d2234ec7e1b9aef77f9d3e481b96db2de7cca470a",
"readout": "quantized last-position logits restricted to declared answer slots; no generated tokens"
}
}

Apply application-level thresholds and fallbacks. Don’t use a model decision as a substitute for authorization.

Clean up
Delete the SageMaker AI endpoint, endpoint configuration, and model:

python deploy/cleanup_endpoint.py \
--region "$AWS_REGION" \
--name "$STANDARD_ENDPOINT_NAME"

python deploy/cleanup_endpoint.py \
--region "$AWS_REGION" \
--name "$SEMIF_ENDPOINT_NAME"

The script deletes only those explicitly named SageMaker AI resources. Delete the CodeBuild projects, ECR repository, model and source objects in Amazon S3, logs, and purpose-specific IAM roles when you no longer need them.
Conclusion
The AWS DLC for llama.cpp gives you a managed foundation for serving decision models on SageMaker AI across CPU and GPU instances. It can load GGUF models from SageMaker AI model artifacts or a configured Hugging Face repository, then serve OpenAI-compatible chat completions through InvokeEndpoint without requiring a custom container. When your application needs direct logits and model state operations, you can extend the DLC with a SemIf adapter. Choose CPU for workloads that aren’t latency-sensitive, and choose GPU when prompt prefill and tail latency affect the application experience.
Review the code sample , AWS DLC for llama.cpp documentation , and SageMaker AI custom inference container contract to adapt the deployment for your workload.

title: Run multi-node inference workloads using Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers
summary: Learn how to deploy one large language model across two GPU nodes on Amazon EKS using the multi-node Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers, with separate prefill and decode nodes behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The pre-built container ships the full inference stack, so you configure the deployment instead of assembling it.
content:
This post shows how to deploy one large language model (LLM) across two GPU nodes on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with the multi-node Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers . It uses separate prefill and decode nodes behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. This kind of multi-node setup is common for tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism, as well as prefill/decode disaggregation inference workloads. In a previous post , we introduced the Ray Serve DLC and used it to stand up a small model behind an HTTP endpoint on a single GPU node. You had a working inference endpoint, and the container keeps the GPU stack compatible, including CUDA libraries, so you did not need to write boilerplate code.
Ray is a distributed compute framework, so Ray Serve deployments can span multiple nodes. Customers use multi-node Ray Serve for several reasons. Some want to run foundation or open-weight models that are too large for a single GPU. Others need more throughput than one replica can deliver. Still others want to separate the two phases of inference to improve performance. In each case, customers must build the dependency chain themselves: choosing compatible libraries for the GPU stack and debugging issues when a component drifts out of alignment. This is undifferentiated work that takes time and effort away from delivering models.
AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) have long solved this kind of problem for training and inferencing workloads. DLCs are pre-built, performance-optimized Docker images that bundle a framework, its dependencies, and the GPU stack into a tested, patched combination you can pull and use immediately. With the launch of the Ray LLM DLC for multi-node deployments, that same approach now extends to multi-node inference. You get a container purpose-built for serving models behind an HTTP endpoint, maintained and tested by AWS, with the full inference stack already assembled.
This post walks through implementing multi-node disaggregated inference using multi-node Ray LLM DLC: deploying a single large language model across two GPU-powered nodes on Amazon EKS cooperating behind a single endpoint. While one of the GPU nodes handles the prefill phase, the other GPU node handles the decode phase. Separating the phases prevents compute-heavy long prompts from stalling token generation for requests already in progress. This approach is well suited for workloads such as Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), document summarization, and agentic applications. We use the multi-node Ray LLM DLC, which ships Ray Serve LLM , NVIDIA Inference Transfer Library (NIXL) , and the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) stack, and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with no application code. The complete code is available in the accompanying repository .
Why prefill/decode (PD) disaggregation
LLM inference has two distinct phases. Prefill processes the entire input prompt in parallel and builds the key-value (KV) cache. Decode then generates the response one token at a time, reading and extending that cache. Prefill is compute bound, and Decode is bound by memory bandwidth. When both phases share one GPU, they contend for the same resources, and the bursty, compute-heavy prefill work interferes with the steady, latency-sensitive decode work. Separating the prefill phase from the decode phase means you can select the hardware and serving properties for each phase, improving overall performance at scale.
PD disaggregation places the two phases on separate nodes, so each phase runs without interfering with the other and can be scaled independently. The trade-off is that the KV cache built during prefill must be handed to the decode node, and that transfer should be fast enough not to erase the benefit. That is exactly why the interconnect between the nodes matters.
What the Ray LLM DLC provides
AWS DLCs are pre-built, performance-optimized Docker images that bundle a framework, its dependencies, and the GPU stack into a tested, patched combination you can pull and use immediately. All components are validated together before each release, so there is no version drift between the CUDA runtime, the framework, and the serving layer. Security patches are applied at build time.
The Ray LLM DLC extends this to distributed LLM serving. It ships vLLM as the inference engine, Ray Serve’s HTTP as the serving layer, NIXL for KV-cache transfer between nodes, and the EFA stack ( libfabric and aws-ofi-nccl ) for high-bandwidth node-to-node communication. Because the Ray Serve LLM library includes a built-in application builder, the entire serving application is a block of YAML. There’s no handler class, no model archiver, and no custom image to build. A single helper, build_pd_openai_app , takes a prefill configuration and a decode configuration and wires the KV-cache transfer between them behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
Architecture
The following diagram shows how the deployment is laid out on Amazon EKS. A user request reaches the Ray head on the CPU system node, and the two GPU worker nodes run the prefill and decode phases of the model.

Figure 1: Multi-node inference architecture on Amazon EKS, with the Ray head on a CPU system node and the prefill and decode phases on two GPU worker nodes

The deployment is an EKS cluster inside a virtual private cloud (VPC). Nodes run in private subnets with outbound access through a NAT Gateway. A CPU system node (m7i.xlarge) hosts system workloads, the KubeRay operator, and the Ray head pod, which is CPU-only. Two GPU worker nodes (g6.8xlarge) run the Ray workers: one serving the prefill phase, and the other serving the decode phase. Both nodes pull the Ray LLM DLC from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) .
KubeRay watches the RayService you apply and wires the head-to-worker join automatically. Ray Serve places the prefill and decode deployments on the two GPU workers. The KV cache flows from the prefill worker to the decode worker over NIXL, using EFA through NIXL’s libfabric backend. The GPU node group is pinned to a single Availability Zone (AZ) because EFA cannot cross AZs.
Prerequisites
To follow along with this post, you need:

An AWS account with billing enabled.
Sufficient service quota for running two g6.8xlarge instances (at least 64 vCPU) in your target Region.
AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) with credentials configured.
kubectl CLI for communicating with a Kubernetes cluster’s control plane.
eksctl CLI for creating and managing clusters on EKS.
helm (package manager for Kubernetes) to install KubeRay operator.
envsubst utility (part of the GNU gettext) to render the manifest.

Verify that your AWS credentials are active with the following command:

aws sts get-caller-identity

Use the pre-built application to serve inference
The application is the serveConfigV2 block in manifest/rayservice.yaml . It uses build_pd_openai_app , which takes a prefill_config and a decode_config and connects the KV-cache transfer between them:

applications:
- name: qwen
import_path: ray.serve.llm:build_pd_openai_app # OpenAI-compatible PD app, built in
route_prefix: /
args:
prefill_config:
model_loading_config: { model_id: qwen3.5-9b, model_source: Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B }
engine_kwargs:
max_model_len: 4096
dtype: bfloat16
gpu_memory_utilization: 0.90
enforce_eager: true # Skip CUDA graph capture to reduce peak GPU memory
kv_transfer_config:
kv_connector: NixlConnector
kv_role: kv_both
engine_id: prefill
kv_connector_extra_config: { backends: ["LIBFABRIC"] }
deployment_config: { num_replicas: 1 }
decode_config:
model_loading_config: { model_id: qwen3.5-9b, model_source: Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B }
engine_kwargs:
max_model_len: 4096
dtype: bfloat16
gpu_memory_utilization: 0.90
enforce_eager: true
kv_transfer_config:
kv_connector: NixlConnector
kv_role: kv_both
engine_id: decode
kv_connector_extra_config: { backends: ["LIBFABRIC"] }
deployment_config: { num_replicas: 1 }

A few settings carry most of the weight. max_model_len: 4096 sizes the context to fit the measured KV cache on the GPU. dtype: bfloat16 and gpu_memory_utilization: 0.90 set precision and how much VRAM vLLM can claim. enforce_eager: true skips CUDA graph capture to reduce peak GPU memory (model- and input-dependent). The kv_transfer_config setting is what makes disaggregation work: both phases use NixlConnector with kv_role: kv_both and a distinct engine_id (prefill on one, decode on the other). The critical setting is kv_connector_extra_config: { backends: ["LIBFABRIC"] } . Without that line, NIXL defaults to UCX, which runs at TCP speed even on EFA.
The rest of the manifest, in rayClusterConfig , describes the pods. The head pod is CPU-only ( num-gpus: "0" ) and pinned to the system node group. Each worker pod requests one GPU and one EFA interface ( nvidia.com/gpu: "1", vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: "1" ) and targets the GPU nodes through nodeSelector: { role: gpu-worker } . It runs privileged: true because NIXL registers CUDA VRAM with the EFA NIC. The IPC_LOCK capability alone isn’t enough. The workers set FI_PROVIDER=efa , read VLLM_HOST_IP from the pod IP, and mount a shared-memory volume. Memory limits sit well above the roughly 18 GiB checkpoint so the OS page cache can hold it. For Qwen3.5-9B model loading on g6.8xlarge with the preceding cache configuration, the model weights loading drops from around 145 seconds to about 2 seconds on restart.
Deploy on Amazon EKS
All scripts share a single configuration file, scripts/env.sh . The script contains defaults for CLUSTER_NAME , REGION , K8S_VERSION , and NAMESPACE . Other defaults cover the system and GPU node groups, the KubeRay version, and the model. Override any variable by exporting it before running a script.
From the project root, set a base directory, then load the variables:

CURRENT_DIR=$(pwd)
cd $CURRENT_DIR/ray-serve-multi-node/scripts
source ./env.sh

Step 1: Create the EKS cluster

./deploy_cluster.sh

This provisions the EKS cluster (VPC, OIDC provider, core add-ons) and a CPU system node group that runs system workloads, the KubeRay operator, and the Ray head. Nodes run in private subnets with egress through a NAT Gateway, and cluster subnets are placed in the AZs that offer the GPU instance type. The script is idempotent and takes 15–20 minutes on a fresh run.
Step 2: Add GPU worker nodes

./deploy_node_group.sh

This creates the GPU node group: two g6.8xlarge instances with EFA enabled, pinned to a single AZ and labeled role=gpu-worker so the Ray workers target them. Enabling EFA also installs the EFA device plugin, which advertises vpc.amazonaws.com/efa on each node. This step takes about 5-20 minutes, usually longer on a first run.
Step 3: Install the KubeRay operator

./install_kuberay.sh

This installs the KubeRay operator using Helm, pinned to the system node group to keep the GPU nodes available for inference. KubeRay watches the RayService you apply next and wires the head-to-worker join automatically. This step takes about 1–2 minutes.
Step 4: Deploy the RayService

./deploy_ray_service.sh

This renders manifest/rayservice.yaml with your image, model, and naming variables using envsubst and applies it. KubeRay creates the head and two worker pods, and Ray Serve LLM brings up the prefill and decode deployments. The script waits for the head to be Ready, both workers to be Running, and finally for the Serve app to report RUNNING. Because each node loads the model, expect this step to take several minutes.
Check status at any time, including which node each pod landed on and the GPU capacity available:

./deploy_ray_service.sh status

Invoke the model
After the Serve app is healthy, KubeRay creates a stable <rayservice-name>-serve-svc Service. Port-forward to it:

kubectl port-forward -n inference svc/ray-llm-serve-svc 8000:8000

Because the DLC exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, you can list models and send a standard chat-completion request with no custom schema:

curl --silent http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models
curl --fail --silent --show-error \
--request POST "http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions" \
--header "Content-Type: application/json" \
--data '{
"model": "qwen3.5-9b",
"messages": [
{"role": "user", "content": "Explain the benefits of prefill/decode disaggregation."}
],
"max_tokens": 200,
"temperature": 0.7
}'

Verify EFA is being used
NIXL falls back to a TCP-speed transport if it cannot use libfabric, and it does so without raising an error, so it’s worth confirming the backend it picked. Grep the worker logs:

for POD in $(kubectl get pods -n inference -l ray.io/node-type=worker \
-o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do
kubectl exec -n inference "$POD" -c ray-worker -- \
grep -rhoE "Backend (LIBFABRIC|UCX) was instantiated" /tmp/ray/session_latest/logs/ 2>/dev/null
done | sort | uniq -c

deploy_node_group.sh already prints the vpc.amazonaws.com/efa count per node when it creates the group. For a cross-node bandwidth number, the DLC ships a prebuilt NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) benchmark at /usr/local/bin/all_reduce_perf .
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, tear down the resources in reverse order:

./delete_ray_service.sh # Remove the RayService
./install_kuberay.sh cleanup # Uninstall the KubeRay operator
./delete_node_group.sh # Remove the GPU node group
./delete_cluster.sh # Delete the EKS cluster

Conclusion and next steps
You served a single model across two GPU nodes with prefill/decode disaggregation, and the entire application was a block of YAML, with no handler code, no model archiver, and no hand-assembled GPU and EFA stack. The multi-node Ray LLM DLC supplied the tested inference stack, KubeRay orchestrated the Ray cluster, and NIXL over EFA carried the KV cache between nodes. Your job was to configure it, not to build it.
Common patterns for running multi-node inference include tensor and pipeline parallelism (sharding a model too big for one instance), data parallelism (replicating a model for throughput), and prefill/decode disaggregation (separating the two phases of inference onto different nodes).
From here you can scale the decode replicas for more throughput, move to larger models with tensor or pipeline parallelism on larger GPU instances, or layer extra libraries onto the same tested base for models that need them. For the full code, the current list of image tags, and the underlying mechanics, see the accompanying repository , the Ray LLM DLC available images page , the Ray Serve LLM prefill/decode documentation , and the EFA documentation .
 

About the authors

Ananth Raghavendra
Ananth is a Senior AI Solutions Architect at AWS. He specializes in architecting distributed Gen AI applications running on NVIDIA GPUs, AWS Trainium and AWS Inferentia using platforms and orchestrators such as Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, Amazon EKS, Ray, SageMaker Serverless Inference, Amazon Nova Forge, and Slurm.

Jinyan Li
Jinyan is a Software Development Engineer at AWS on the Deep Learning Containers team, where she builds and maintains the ML container images that ship PyTorch, vLLM, Ray, and other frameworks to customers running workloads on Amazon SageMaker, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), and Amazon EKS, including the Ray LLM DLC used in this post.

Felipe is a Principal AI/ML Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS. Prior to joining AWS, Felipe worked with GE Digital and SLB, where he focused on modeling and optimization products for industrial applications.

light_analysis.summary: AWS 发布 Ray LLM Deep Learning Container（DLC），支持在 Amazon EKS 上把单个大语言模型拆分到两个 GPU 节点部署，实现预填充（Prefill）与解码（Decode）分离推理。容器预置 vLLM、Ray Serve LLM、NIXL 和 EFA 网络栈，通过 build_pd_openai_app 以一段 YAML 直接暴露 OpenAI 兼容接口，无需编写 handler 或自定义镜像。分离让计算密集的预填充与访存密集的解码互不干扰、可独立扩展，适用于 RAG、文档摘要和 Agent 类负载。KV 缓存经 NIXL+EFA 在节点间传输，若不显式指定 LIBFABRIC 后端则会退回 TCP 速度。
